story: In the fifth century a singing school, the Schola Cantorum, was founded in Rome, while Gaul kept its own Gallican chant and Italy an Old Roman chant. During a visit to Gaul in 752–753 Pope Stephen II said Mass with Roman chant, and Pepin abolished the local Gallican rites in favour of the Roman use, to strengthen ties with Rome. In 785–786, at Charlemagne's request, Pope Adrian I sent a papal sacramentary with Roman chants to the Carolingian court, and a project overseen by Chrodegang of Metz promoted the Roman Mass across Francia. Scholars date this blend of Roman and Gallican chant to around 750; it was fitted into what became the eight church modes. The Metz project also invented neumes, free-form signs showing the shape of a remembered melody. Charlemagne spread the chant through his empire to consolidate religious and secular power, and by the 9th century Gallican chant had effectively been eliminated. The first manuscripts with notation date from around 930, many of them from Regensburg, St. Gall, Laon and St. Martial. Improvised harmonizations of the chant, called organum, opened the way to medieval polyphony, and modern staff notation grew directly from its neumes.

story: Islamic tradition holds that Muhammad received his first revelation in 610 in the Cave of Hira, and further revelations over 23 years. The first muezzin was Bilal ibn Rabah, a freed slave of Abyssinian heritage chosen for his loud voice; at the conquest of Mecca in 630 he called the prayer from the Kaaba. In the following generation, reciters in Mecca, Medina, Kufa, Basra and Syria became known as teachers, and their ways of reading took their names. Under the Abbasids, as many non-Arabs became Muslims and mispronunciation spread, scholars began writing down the rules, and Abu Ubaid al-Qasim bin Salam (774–838) was the first to set tajwid in writing. Abu Bakr Ibn Mujahid (859–936) limited the accepted readings to seven. In the adhan each phrase is followed by a longer pause and grows longer and more ornamented on repetition; Medina uses maqam Bayati, Mecca maqam Hijaz. In 1944 Mahmoud Khalil Al-Hussary won Egyptian Radio's reciters' competition, and became the first to record the whole Quran in the measured murattal style. Abdul Basit Abdus-Samad, known for the melodic mujawwad style, joined Egyptian Radio in 1951, and his recitations were broadcast by radio stations in other Arab countries.

story: From the 5th century, music and dance reached Japan from mainland China and the Korean peninsula; in 554 musicians are said to have come from the Korean kingdom of Baekje. In 701 the Taihō Code set up the Gagaku-ryō, a court bureau for music and dance. In 736 the monk Buttetsu brought Rin'yū music, said to come from India and Southeast Asia; in 752 Tang, Korean and native dances marked the eye-opening of the Great Buddha at Tōdai-ji in Nara. In the 9th and 10th centuries the Heian court fused these imported styles with native song, and split the repertoire into a left side built on Tang music and a right side built on Korean music. Courtiers played too: Minamoto no Hiromasa is remembered for the flute and biwa, Fujiwara no Moronaga as a biwa master. After the Ōnin War of 1467 to 1477 the ensembles stopped playing in Kyoto for about 100 years, until the Tokugawa shogunate revived them. After 1868 the guilds of Osaka, Nara and Kyoto moved to Tokyo, where their descendants make up most of the Imperial Palace Music Department. In 1973 Tōru Takemitsu completed Shuteiga (In an Autumn Garden) for the Imperial Household ensemble.

story: In the 13th century Sharangadeva wrote the Sangita Ratnakara, whose raga names such as Turushka Todi ("Turkish Todi") show ideas arriving from Islamic culture; it is the last text cited by both the Hindustani and Carnatic traditions. Under the Delhi Sultanate and then the Mughals, musicians found patrons in the new rulers' courts, and Hindu and Muslim ideas met in new forms such as qawwali and khyal. Amir Khusrau (1253–1325), a disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya of Delhi who composed in Persian, Turkish, Arabic and Braj Bhasha, is credited with introducing ragas such as Yaman Kalyan. At Gwalior, Raja Man Singh Tomar (1486–1516) moved classical song from Sanskrit into Hindi, and dhrupad developed at his court. In 1562 Tansen joined the court of the Mughal emperor Akbar, where he introduced new ragas and compositions. When the Mughal Empire broke up, smaller courts such as Oudh, Patiala and Banaras kept paying musicians, and their family styles became the gharanas. In 1901 Vishnu Digambar Paluskar opened the Gandharva Mahavidyalaya school in Lahore, and between 1909 and 1932 Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande sorted the ragas into thaats. Fred Gaisberg's first recordings of Indian music, in 1902, made Gauhar Jan the music's first star.

story: From the 12th century, Persian and Islamic influence in North India pulled Indian classical music into two styles, and by the 16th and 17th centuries the southern Carnatic style stood apart from Hindustani music. Purandara Dasa (1484–1564) set the graded exercises by which it is still traditionally taught, starting beginners on the raga Mayamalavagowla. In the 18th and 19th centuries its main patrons were the Maratha rulers of Tanjore and the kings of Mysore and Travancore. Three contemporaries, Tyagaraja (1767–1847), Muthuswami Dikshitar (1776–1835) and Syama Sastri (1762–1827), became known as its Trinity. Tyagaraja, whose father worked at the court of Thuljaji, spent most of his life in Thiruvaiyaru and turned down King Serfoji II's invitation to court; about 720 of his songs, in Sanskrit and Telugu, survive. At Fort St. George in Madras, Dikshitar and his brothers heard Western orchestral music and the violin, and his brother Balaswami brought the violin into Carnatic music. Musicians founded the Tyagaraja Aradhana festival at Thiruvaiyaru in 1846, and by the late 19th century Madras had become the music's centre. When the princely states dissolved around independence in 1947, patronage passed to private societies called sabhas that sold tickets to concerts.

story: Georgian villagers were singing in parts before Christianity reached Georgia at the start of the 4th century. From the 7th and 8th centuries, Georgian church composers translated Greek Orthodox chants and added harmonies to the single-line melodies. Village singers, mostly farmers, kept the tradition going for centuries. In Kakheti, table songs set two soloists over a long drone bass; in Guria, three or four singers each took a separate line, with a yodel called krimanchuli. As farm work changed, the supra feast became where many kinds of song survived. The first professional choir, formed in 1886, began moving singers toward Western tuning. Under Soviet rule (1921–1991) church songs were forbidden, and huge regional choirs cut back the singers' improvising. In 1968 Anzor Erkomaishvili founded the Rustavi Choir; the Kakhetian song Chakrulo went into space on the Voyager records in 1977, and UNESCO listed Georgian polyphonic singing in 2001.

story: Hourglass talking drums are among the oldest instruments of West African griots, traced back to the Bono, the Yoruba, the Ghana Empire and the Hausa. Yoruba tradition names Ayangalu as the first drummer, made a deity at his death, and families whose names begin with Ayan are the hereditary keepers of his craft. The batá drum, dated to roughly 500 years ago, is said to have been introduced by a Yoruba king named Shango, and was played for gods, royalty and ancestors. In a dundun ensemble the leader, the oniyalu, makes the drum talk by copying the three main tones of the Yoruba language. Under the drums an iron bell sounds a seven-stroke key pattern. Drummers sent warnings of attacks and news of ceremonies between villages, which Europeans noticed in the first half of the 18th century. The slave trade brought almost 300,000 Africans to Cuba, where an enslaved Yoruba man named Añabi made the first sacred batá around 1830. In the 20th century the talking drum entered Nigerian jùjú and fuji, and in 1959 Babatunde Olatunji, born in Ajido near Badagry, released Drums of Passion on the Columbia label.

story: Maracatu nação grew out of the crowning of Kings of Congo, enslaved people given leadership roles in the enslaved community by the Portuguese administration. Its oldest record, from Pernambuco, dates to 1711. In Recife on 15 November 1800 an enslaved man, Manuel Santiago, broke with Maracatu Brilhante and founded Maracatu Elefante, later the first nation led by a woman. When Brazil abolished slavery in 1888 the Kings of Congo ended, but the nations kept choosing symbolic leaders and staging their coronations. They parade with 80 to 100 drummers on rope-tuned alfaias and a gonguê bell, behind a king and queen dressed as the Portuguese Baroque court. Between the late 19th and early 20th centuries, sugarcane cutters on the plantations of Nazaré da Mata created maracatu rural, also called maracatu de trombone. Around 1991 Chico Science, from Olinda's Rio Doce neighbourhood, co-founded the Mangue Bit movement, and his band Chico Science & Nação Zumbi fused maracatu with rock, funk and hip hop. In the 1990s Maracatu Nação Pernambuco took the genre to overseas audiences, and groups now play it in cities including Lisbon and Toronto.

story: Gnawa music grew from the traditions of West Africans, among them Hausa, Fulani and Bambara people, carried to Morocco by the trans-Saharan slave trade. It took shape in the 16th and 17th centuries, and its songs still keep West African words and speak of abduction, suffering and privation. At the lila, a ritual that runs from late evening until sunrise, a maalem plays the three-string guembri and calls the spirits while his troupe clacks heavy iron qraqeb castanets. The night runs through seven suites, one for each family of spirits, called mluk, each with its own colour, incense, rhythm and dance. Other Moroccan brotherhoods open with their founding saint's Arabic texts; the Gnawa, whose ancestors did not read Arabic, open instead by singing of their enslaved forebears. Since 1998 the Gnaoua World Music Festival in Essaouira has put maalems on stage with Randy Weston, Pharoah Sanders and other jazz musicians. Maalem Mahmoud Guinia, born in 1951, played with Pharoah Sanders and Carlos Santana. In 2019 UNESCO inscribed Gnawa on its list of the intangible heritage of humanity.

story: In late Renaissance Florence, a circle of humanists and musicians meeting under Count Giovanni de' Bardi, the Camerata, rejected the many-voiced polyphony of their day and looked to ancient Greek drama. In 1598 Jacopo Peri and the poet Ottavio Rinuccini staged Dafne, sung throughout, and in 1600 Peri's Euridice followed, the earliest surviving opera. Singers were now backed by a basso continuo: a keyboard player read figures written above the bass line and improvised the chords. Claudio Monteverdi, composer of L'Orfeo, auditioned in 1613 for the post of maestro at San Marco in Venice and held it until his death. Trading cities wanted opera houses paid for by subscription, and in 1637 Venice opened San Cassiano, the first public opera house in Europe. Heinrich Schütz took the Venetian style to Germany, and Jean-Baptiste Lully bought patents to be the French king's sole composer of operas. Arcangelo Corelli published concerti grossi that set a full orchestra against a smaller group, and his pupil Antonio Vivaldi wrote hundreds of works on that model. Italian composers moved to the galant style around 1730, while Johann Sebastian Bach kept to the Baroque manner until 1750, and the galant style led into the Classical period.

story: The ghazal began as Arabic love poetry in the 7th century, entered Persian in the 10th, and reached the Indian subcontinent in the 12th with the courts of a new Islamic sultanate. In the 13th century Amir Khusrow began writing it in the local Hindavi tongue, putting Persian verse forms into local speech. In the 18th century poets such as Mir Taqi Mir, born in Agra in 1723, moved the ghazal from Persian into Urdu. Poets lived on court patronage, and the state of Oudh paid so well that many moved to Lucknow, Farrukhabad and Faizabad. After Ahmad Shah Abdali sacked Delhi each year from 1748, Mir went to Lucknow in 1782 at the invitation of Asaf-ud-Daulah. In Delhi the Red Fort hosted mushaira gatherings and paid poets such as Ghalib, until the rebellion of 1857 ended that patronage. Akhtari Bai Faizabadi, born in 1914 and later called Begum Akhtar, put ghazals on gramophone records and was among the first women to sing them in public concerts, not private gatherings. In the 20th century she, the Pakistani singer Mehdi Hassan and Jagjit Singh brought Western instruments such as the guitar into the ghazal, and film songs spread it.

story: The koto had been kept to the court, tuned to gagaku, and the shamisen descended from the Chinese sanxian, which reached Japan in the 16th century through the Ryukyu Kingdom and the port of Sakai. Yatsuhashi Kengyo (1614–1685), a blind Kyoto shamisen player, learned the koto from a court musician and first taught it to the public. He replaced the six old koto songs with a new form, kumiuta, and retuned the koto to scales taken from shamisen music. In the Edo period, monks of the Fuke Zen sect, the komuso, walked Japan playing the shakuhachi as meditation and begging for alms, exempt from the shogun's travel limits. The Meiji Restoration of 1868 abolished the shogunate and the Fuke sect, and the shakuhachi was allowed back only to accompany koto and shamisen, later taking the kokyu's place in the trio called sankyoku. Michio Miyagi, born in Kobe in 1894 and blind from the age of eight, joined Western music to the koto, wrote Haru no Umi in 1929 and built a 17-string bass koto. In 1932 the French violinist Renée Chemet arranged its shakuhachi part for violin and recorded it with Miyagi for Japan and Europe.

story: Romani migrants reached Andalusia in the 15th century and met the Arab-Andalusian music already there. In 1783 King Carlos III issued a decree that improved the legal position of Spain's gitanos. Flamenco took shape at the end of the 18th century in the cities and farm towns of lower Andalusia, and its first written trace comes from Jerez de la Frontera. It was made by three or four dozen gitano families together with Andalusia's urban poor and journeymen. In 1881 the singer Silverio Franconetti opened a flamenco café in Seville where singers competed in public, and out of it came the professional cantaor. Local singers there reworked Andalusian folk songs in their own style, and the paying public's taste pulled technique and themes into one shared form. From 1920 to 1955 promoters staged it in bullrings and theatres as "flamenco opera", and in 1922 Manuel de Falla and Federico García Lorca answered with a cante jondo contest in Granada open only to amateurs. In the flamenco fusion of the 1970s, guitarist Paco de Lucía from Algeciras and singer Camarón de la Isla broke with Antonio Mairena's conservatism, and Paco de Lucía brought in Brazilian music, Arabic music and jazz.

story: Before it, publishers mostly printed European songs to avoid royalties; only about 10 to 30 percent of music printed in the United States was by American composers. After the Civil War, middle-class families owned pianos and bought sheet music to play new songs at home. From about 1885 publishers gathered in one Manhattan district, and by the late 1890s most had followed Witmark to West 28th Street between Fifth and Sixth Avenues. Many publishers were former salesmen or Jewish immigrants: Leo Feist had sold corsets, Edward B. Marks buttons. Charles K. Harris wrote "After the Ball" in 1892, Irving Berlin "Alexander's Ragtime Band" in 1911. Publishers paid song pluggers, George Gershwin among them, to play new songs in music stores and sell the sheet music. They began with ballads and comic songs, took up the cakewalk and ragtime, later jazz and blues, always in a form amateur singers and small-town bands could play from print. From the 1930s the phonograph, radio and film replaced sheet music as the driving force, and in the 1950s rock and roll, centred on the Brill Building, took over. In 1985 Bob Dylan said he had ended it: "People can record their own songs now."

story: In 1810 E. T. A. Hoffmann reviewed Beethoven's Fifth Symphony and set out the principles of musical Romanticism, holding instrumental music to be the art best suited to expressing emotion. Composers had lived under aristocratic patronage; now they increasingly wrote for public concerts with large paying audiences. The move away from Viennese classicism ran through the work of Beethoven and of Franz Schubert, whose Erlkönig is among the first Romantic lieder. In 1821 Carl Maria von Weber's Der Freischütz became the first German Romantic opera. Its centres lay in Berlin, Dresden and Leipzig, where Felix Mendelssohn took over the Gewandhaus Orchestra in 1835 and founded a conservatory in 1843. Better valves and keys from the Industrial Revolution made wind instruments more reliable, and Hector Berlioz enlarged the orchestra. Franz Liszt, a Hungarian piano virtuoso, created the symphonic poem: one movement built on a theme, character or literary text. Richard Wagner took chromatic harmony to its extreme in Tristan und Isolde, and from 1876 the Bayreuth Festival staged only his works. As Romanticism came apart, Arnold Schoenberg and the Second Viennese School answered with Expressionism, and in France Claude Debussy's Pelléas and Mélisande of 1902 carried music towards Impressionism.

story: Spirituals grew from African musical traditions blended with Christian hymns brought by missionaries and slaveholders to enslaved Africans in the American South. The revivals of the First Great Awakening in the 1730s and 1740s converted many enslaved people. The songs first flourished in secret meetings, the hush harbors, and later spread to camp meetings and revivals. They stayed oral until 1867, when the abolitionists Charles Pickard Ware, Lucy McKim Garrison and William Francis Allen printed Slave Songs of the United States, with songs Ware took down from the Gullah people of South Carolina's Port Royal Islands. On 6 October 1871 nine students of the new Fisk school in Nashville, Tennessee, set out as the Fisk Jubilee Singers to raise money for it. At first they left out the slave songs, sacred to their parents; then the Reverend Alexander Reid gave them "Swing Low, Sweet Chariot", learned from Wallace and Minerva Willis, enslaved by the Choctaw. By 1872 they sang at the White House, and in 1873 they toured Europe. Harry Burleigh made spirituals into art songs for solo concert singers. Blues and gospel grew from the spirituals, and civil rights freedom songs such as "Oh, Freedom!" were adapted from them.

story: Tango grew from the payada, the milonga of the Argentine and Uruguayan pampas, and Uruguayan candombe, which had been practised in Argentina since the first enslaved Africans were brought there. The first tango group was two Afro-Argentines, Casimiro Alcorta on violin and Sinforoso on clarinet, who played small concerts in Buenos Aires from the early 1870s to the early 1890s. European immigrants played early tango in Buenos Aires and Montevideo. Ángel Villoldo wrote "El Choclo" in 1903 and recorded it himself in Paris, because Argentina had no recording studios. In the 1920s tango moved out of the brothels, and the bandleaders Roberto Firpo and Francisco Canaro dropped the flute and put a double bass in its place. Carlos Gardel helped develop the sung tango canción in the 1920s, and his Spanish-language films for Paramount in the early 1930s fed Argentina's new sound-film industry. In the Golden Age, from about 1935 to 1952, tango was played by orquestas típicas of over a dozen players, among them those of Juan d'Arienzo, Francisco Canaro and Aníbal Troilo. In the 1950s Ástor Piazzolla set out to break tango's classic forms, and he and his followers built nuevo tango from jazz and classical elements.

story: Admiral José Prudencio Padilla wrote that on the night of 18 June 1821 Indigenous people in Arjona greeted the feast of Saint John with gaitas and cumbiambas. In Santa Marta in 1825–26 the Swedish naval lieutenant Carl August Gosselman saw a street dance played on a bamboo flute like a gaita, a maraca and a drum from a fire-hollowed trunk. In Barranquilla in 1888 a woman known as La Cañón set up large cumbiamba circles at the four corners of Bolívar street, danced to drums and flutes. Cumbia had been instrumental; in time, singers were added. Clarinetist Lucho Bermúdez, who grew up in El Carmen de Bolívar, wrote stylized orchestral arrangements of cumbia, and by the 1940s it was spreading from the coast to the rest of Colombia. Record companies on the coast, among them Discos Fuentes, founded in 1934, helped carry it abroad. In 1946 Bermúdez recorded 60 of his compositions for RCA Víctor in Argentina. In Mexico in the 1940s the Colombian singer Luis Carlos Meyer and orchestra director Rafael de Paz made La Cumbia Cienaguera, considered the first cumbia recorded outside Colombia. In 1960s Peru, Los Destellos were among the first to lead cumbia with electric guitars.

story: The bolero did not come from the Italian opera and canzone then popular in Havana, but from romantic folk poetry sung by a new kind of troubadour in Santiago de Cuba, the trovadores. These itinerant musicians travelled around Oriente province and earned their living by singing and playing the guitar. Pepe Sánchez, born in Santiago de Cuba in 1856, wrote the first bolero, "Tristezas", in 1883. He had no formal training, composed in his head and never wrote his songs down, so most of them are lost. Trovadores who first sang alone with a guitar began to play as duos, trios and quartets. In 1905 the tenor Adolfo Colombo recorded the bolero "La Dorila", through the trovador Sindo Garay, who settled in Havana the next year. Around 1915 the first radio stations spread the bolero in Puerto Rico and Mexico, where Agustín Lara and María Grever wrote boleros of their own. In the 1930s Trío Matamoros mixed it with son into bolero-son, which in the United States became the ballroom rhumba. From the late 1940s, filin singers such as César Portillo de la Luz and José Antonio Méndez turned the bolero toward jazz-influenced crooning.
